questions.q: In fanout-on-write, what happens at the moment a user publishes a post?
options: Followers' clients pull the post the next time the app opens
The post is ranked lazily whenever each follower requests a feed
The post is cached once in a global store and merged into each follower's feed at read time
The post ID is inserted into every follower's precomputed feed store
questions.explanation: Push fanout does the work at write time: one insert per follower into their materialized feed list, so a later read is a single cheap lookup.

questions.q: What is the primary advantage of fanout-on-read (the pull model)?
options: Feed reads complete with a single key lookup per user
Posting is cheap, and no work is wasted on inactive followers
It removes the need for a separate ranking service entirely
It provides stronger ordering guarantees than push-based models
questions.explanation: Pull writes once and computes only when someone actually reads, so a post by a user with millions of dormant followers costs almost nothing at publish time.

questions.q: What does a precomputed per-user feed cache typically contain?
options: Fully rendered HTML for each post in the feed
Complete post bodies with their media attachments stored inline for single-lookup reads
Post IDs, with content hydrated from a post store at read time
Follower graph edges used as inputs for ranking
questions.explanation: Storing only IDs keeps the per-user list tiny and avoids duplicating post bodies millions of times; edits and deletes also apply once in the post store.

questions.q: What is the celebrity problem in news feed design?
options: A single post triggering millions of per-follower feed writes
Celebrities' own feeds becoming too long to paginate efficiently
Hot celebrity posts evicting everything else from the feed cache
Celebrities following too many accounts to merge at read time
questions.explanation: Push fanout cost scales with follower count, so one post from an account with tens of millions of followers becomes a massive write burst and delivery lag.

questions.q: What is the standard hybrid solution to the celebrity problem?
options: Push fanout for most users, pull-and-merge for celebrity authors
Pull for most users, with push fanout reserved for celebrities
Rate limiting how often celebrity accounts are allowed to post
Dedicated shards that replicate celebrity feeds synchronously worldwide
questions.explanation: Ordinary authors keep the cheap-read push path, while high-fanout accounts are excluded from fanout and merged in at read time, capping the worst-case write burst.

questions.q: Why is cursor-based pagination preferred over offset pagination for feeds?
options: Offsets cannot exceed ten thousand rows in most database engines
Cursors compress into shorter URLs than numeric offsets do
New items shift offsets, causing duplicates or gaps; cursors anchor to a stable position
Offset-based queries cannot be cached anywhere at the edge
questions.explanation: Feeds get new items inserted at the head constantly, which slides every offset. A cursor names a position in the sort order, so the next page resumes exactly where it left off.

questions.q: Which storage system is the canonical choice for per-user precomputed feed lists?
options: A relational table joined against the follow graph on every read
An object storage bucket holding one feed file per user
A columnar warehouse optimized for large analytical scans
An in-memory store like Redis sorted sets keyed by user ID
questions.explanation: A sorted set gives ordered inserts, ranged reads, and trimming to a fixed length in memory, matching the feed's access pattern at sub-millisecond latency.

questions.q: In a modern ranked feed pipeline, what is the typical order of stages?
options: Scoring, then candidate generation, then filtering at the end
Candidate generation, filtering, scoring, then diversity re-ranking
Diversity re-ranking first, scoring next, then candidate retrieval as the final stage
Filtering, diversity re-ranking, retrieval, and scoring last
questions.explanation: The funnel narrows progressively: retrieve many candidates cheaply, drop ineligible ones, run the expensive model on what survives, then adjust the final ordering for variety.

questions.q: Why do feed services perform fanout through an async queue of workers rather than synchronously in the post request?
options: Queues automatically deduplicate posts before they reach followers
Synchronous fanout would corrupt the ranking model's features
The post request returns fast while workers absorb the write burst
Async fanout provides exactly-once delivery guarantees to feeds
questions.explanation: Decoupling keeps user-visible publish latency independent of follower count, and the queue buffers spikes so workers can drain at a sustainable rate.

questions.q: Why skip fanout writes entirely for followers who have been inactive for months?
options: Their feed caches would eventually exceed per-key size limits
Stale feeds would skew the ranking model's engagement features
Fanout to inactive users creates hot partitions and memory pressure in the cache tier
The writes are wasted; rebuild their feed by pull if they ever return
questions.explanation: Most fanout targets never read, so the write and the memory it holds are pure waste. A one-time pull rebuild on return is far cheaper than continuous maintenance.

questions.q: A user opens the app and their precomputed feed cache entry was evicted. What happens?
options: The service pulls followees' recent posts, merges and ranks them, then repopulates the cache
The user sees an empty feed until newly created posts arrive
The service replays the entire historical fanout log from the start
The request is rerouted to a replica that still holds the cache
questions.explanation: The cache is an optimization, not the source of truth: on a miss the service falls back to the pull path and rebuilds the entry for subsequent reads.

questions.q: A user posts and immediately refreshes, but their own post is missing from the feed. What is the standard fix?
options: Switch the entire feed path to strongly consistent quorum reads
Ensure read-your-writes by injecting the author's own posts at read time
Reduce the fanout queue's batch size so writes land sooner
Invalidate every CDN cache entry each time a user posts
questions.explanation: Merging the author's own recent posts at read time gives read-your-writes for the one case users notice, without making the whole eventually-consistent pipeline strongly consistent.

questions.q: A post goes viral and its ID hammers one post-store partition. What is the standard mitigation?
options: Migrate the viral post's row onto a larger dedicated shard
Replicate the hot post across cache nodes and add local in-process caches
Disable caching for viral posts so the load spreads to replicas
Reshard the post's row by follower ID to distribute the reads
questions.explanation: A single key cannot be split by sharding, so you replicate it: multi-node cache copies plus a short-TTL in-process cache absorb reads before they reach the partition.

questions.q: In the hybrid model, how do celebrity posts end up in a follower's feed response?
options: Nightly batch jobs append them to every follower's cached feed
The client fetches a public celebrity feed from the CDN and interleaves it
The service merges the precomputed feed with recent posts from followed celebrities at read time
They overwrite the oldest entries of each follower's push feed
questions.explanation: Since celebrity posts were deliberately not fanned out, the read path fetches their recent posts directly and merges them into the cached list before ranking.

questions.q: Why cap each precomputed feed at a few hundred entries?
options: It bounds cache memory, since deep scrolls are rare and can fall back to pull
Ranking models cannot score candidate sets larger than a few hundred
Redis sorted sets degrade sharply once they pass roughly five hundred entries per key
Longer feed lists break cursor pagination beyond the cap
questions.explanation: Memory cost is per-user times entries across hundreds of millions of users, and almost nobody scrolls past the first few hundred items, so trimming is nearly free in practice.

questions.q: The same reshared article appears five times in a user's candidate set from different followees. Which stage should collapse these?
options: Candidate generation, by refusing to retrieve reshared posts from the follow graph at all
The client, by hiding repeated URLs after they render
The fanout workers, by skipping all reshare writes upstream
A dedup step in filtering, collapsing duplicates before scoring
questions.explanation: Deduping in the filter stage removes redundancy before the expensive scoring pass and keeps the final slate correct, rather than papering over it in the client.

questions.q: A network has 100M daily users averaging 200 followers and 2 posts per day. Roughly how many feed-cache writes does full push fanout generate daily?
options: About 400 million
About 4 billion
About 40 billion
About 400 billion
questions.explanation: 100M users x 2 posts = 200M posts per day, and each fans out to 200 followers: 200M x 200 = 40 billion writes, which is why full push fanout needs a hybrid escape hatch.

questions.q: Why can't final feed ranking simply be precomputed at write time during fanout?
options: Scores depend on read-time context and recency decay, so write-time ranking goes stale
Write-time ranking needs the follow graph, which fanout workers cannot access
Precomputed ranking scores cannot be represented in sorted set entries
Ranking during fanout roughly doubles the write amplification, which cache clusters cannot absorb
questions.explanation: Ranking depends on when the user opens the app, what they just saw, and engagement accumulated since publish, none of which are known at write time.

questions.q: The fanout queue develops a growing backlog because workers lag behind. What symptom do users observe?
options: Posting fails with timeouts for every user until the backlog drains
Feed read latency grows in proportion to the queue backlog depth
Duplicate copies of the same post start appearing in feeds
Posts appear in followers' feeds with growing delay while posting itself stays fast
questions.explanation: The queue decouples publish from delivery, so the write path stays healthy and the backlog surfaces purely as increasing propagation delay into followers' feeds.

questions.q: A user blocks an author, but that author's older entries remain in the user's precomputed feed cache. What is the standard handling?
options: Rewrite all affected feed caches synchronously inside the block request
Keep cache entries but apply block-list filtering at read time
Flush every user's feed cache so the author is fully purged
Delete the blocked author's posts from the central post store
questions.explanation: Read-time filtering enforces visibility rules immediately and correctly for every future read, without an expensive scan-and-rewrite of materialized feeds on each block.
